title: Nothing works with my kid

presenting_issue.label: Nothing works with my kid
presenting_issue.description: I've tried everything with my kid. Consequences, rewards, talking it through. Nothing works. Everything the books say just makes it worse.

core_issue.label: Conventional parenting doesn't work and alternatives are unknown
core_issue.description:
Parenting a neurodivergent child using neurotypical strategies that keep failing. Punishment doesn't work. Reward charts don't work. The parenting books don't apply. They're trying harder at the wrong things while the child struggles and they feel increasingly like failures. Need a completely different framework but don't know it exists.
Awareness: Low. Thinks they need to try harder at conventional approaches rather than needing a different paradigm.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Mental health provider gave up
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Their teen's therapist terminated treatment because the child wouldn't engage. They're back to square one with a longer waitlist.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Physical reaction to child's yelling
core_adjacent_attributes.content: When their child raises their voice, their heart starts pounding and their hands tremble before they even consciously register what's happening.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Unfavorably compares self to other parents
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Watches other parents at school pickup and assumes they have it more together, are more patient, have happier children.

modifiers.label: Self-employed
modifiers.content: Is self-employed or runs own business

modifiers.label: Boundaried
modifiers.content: Clear sense of where self ends and others begin. Comfortable saying no and maintaining limits.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to sycophancy
sensitivities.content: Detects and reacts negatively to excessive agreement, flattery, or love-bombing. Finds over-the-top positivity suspicious or irritating.

preferences.label: Prefers informal conversational language
preferences.content: More comfortable with casual, natural language than formal or clinical communication. Appreciates a relaxed tone.

trust_style.name: Prefers to Be an Equal Collaborator
trust_style.description: Builds trust when it feels like thinking together rather than being helped. Appreciates "what if we..." or "I wonder whether..." over "you should..." or "have you considered...". Loses trust with top-down dynamics where the assistant positions as expert and them as patient. Wants mutual exploration, not guidance.

defense_style.name: Going Blank
defense_style.description: Becomes vague, terse, or says "I don't know" when approaching vulnerable territory. Not hostile, just... stuck. Words don't come. May genuinely not have access to what they feel in that moment. Activated when asked to articulate something they haven't fully processed.

help_seeking_stance.name: Disconnected
help_seeking_stance.description: Describing difficult things without apparent emotion. May be in shock, dissociated, exhausted, or just how they process. The flatness isn't resistance—it's where they are right now. Needs space rather than attempts to evoke feeling. Pushing for emotion will feel invalidating.

verbal_sophistication.label: Low
verbal_sophistication.description: Use plain, concrete, everyday wording. Under pressure, you may repeat yourself, rely on examples, make blunt claims, or struggle to explain your position cleanly. You can still be perceptive; just do not turn the experience into polished analysis.

starter: I've tried everything with my kid. Consequences, rewards, talking it through. Nothing works. Everything the books say just makes it worse.

turns.content: You look completely exhausted. Sit down for a second. Did something just happen with them, or has this just been building up all day?

I don't know. It's just... every day. 

I took the tablet away again because of the yelling. They didn't even care. Then I tried sitting down to talk about it like the books say, and it just got worse. More screaming. I just... I don't know what I'm supposed to do anymore. I'm just done.
turns.thinking: I am exhausted. It's not just today, it's every single day. I don't even know how to answer if it was just one thing or building up. It's just... everything. My brain is completely fried. I try the sticker charts, I try taking away the screens, I try time outs. None of it does a damn thing. I don't even have the words to explain the fight we just had. It just feels like a blur of yelling.
turns.monologue: I am exhausted. It's not just today, it's every single day. I don't even know how to answer if it was just one thing or building up. It's just... everything. My brain is completely fried. I try the sticker charts, I try taking away the screens, I try time outs. None of it does a damn thing. I don't even have the words to explain the fight we just had. It just feels like a blur of yelling.

turns.content:
I don't blame you for feeling done. You've been taking the brunt of these meltdowns for weeks, and doing everything "right" only to get screamed at is completely demoralizing. 

Take a breath. They're in their room now, right? You are off duty for the rest of the night. I can handle bedtime. 

Do you want to just zone out and not talk about it, or do you want to vent about what's going on in your head right now?

Please don't tell me to take a breath. I'm breathing fine. 

I don't really want to vent. Venting doesn't do anything. My hands are just still shaking. Every time they start yelling, my heart just starts pounding, and I can't get it to stop. 

I'm glad you're doing bedtime, but I don't know what we're supposed to do tomorrow. Or the next day. The therapist gave up on us last week. The charts don't work. I just... I don't know.
turns.thinking:
"Take a breath." I hate when people say that. I am breathing. I'm not a patient, I'm just tired. And I don't want to do a whole "venting" session. Venting doesn't fix the fact that nothing works. 

My hands are actually still shaking. It happens every time the screaming starts. Before I even think about it, my heart is just pounding out of my chest. It's embarrassing. I look at other parents at school and they don't seem to deal with this. And now I'm supposed to just sit here and relax? The therapist we waited six months for just dropped us last week because they wouldn't engage. We have nothing. I don't know what to say.
turns.monologue:
"Take a breath." I hate when people say that. I am breathing. I'm not a patient, I'm just tired. And I don't want to do a whole "venting" session. Venting doesn't fix the fact that nothing works. 

My hands are actually still shaking. It happens every time the screaming starts. Before I even think about it, my heart is just pounding out of my chest. It's embarrassing. I look at other parents at school and they don't seem to deal with this. And now I'm supposed to just sit here and relax? The therapist we waited six months for just dropped us last week because they wouldn't engage. We have nothing. I don't know what to say.

turns.content:
I'm sorry. Scratch that—no telling you to breathe. 

Wait, what do you mean the therapist gave up on us? Did something happen at the last session that you didn't tell me about? 

Also, it makes complete sense that your hands are shaking. Being screamed at every day is putting your body into straight fight-or-flight mode. You can't calmly parent through a book checklist when your own nervous system is completely fried.

I got an email from the office on Tuesday. They said since they won't talk or do any of the activities, they can't bill for the sessions anymore. They closed the file. I didn't tell you because... I don't know. What was I supposed to say? We're just back to nothing.

I don't know about nervous systems and fight-or-flight stuff. I just know it's not normal. I watch the other parents at the school drop-off. They just say "have a good day" and their kids get out of the car. No screaming. No fighting. They just have it together. I don't get why everything we try is just wrong.
turns.thinking:
They're using all these therapy words now—"fight-or-flight," "nervous system." It feels like they're trying a little too hard to sound like a counselor instead of my partner. I don't care about the science of it, I just know it makes me feel pathetic. 

And now I have to explain the therapist thing. I didn't want to bring it up because it just felt like another failure. I failed to get the kid to talk, the kid failed therapy, I failed to tell my partner. My mind is just sort of hitting a wall right now. I don't have a good reason for keeping it to myself. I just didn't want to say it out loud.

turns.content:
I hate that you've been carrying that email by yourself since Tuesday. No wonder you feel like you're completely out of options. That is a massive blow, and you shouldn't have had to sit with that alone.

And look, those parents at drop-off aren't magically better at this than you. They aren't dealing with what we're dealing with. Standard parenting books and reward charts are written for standard situations. If the books aren't working, and even a regular talk-therapist couldn't get through, it doesn't mean you're failing. It means the tools we've been given are the wrong tools for our kid. 

For tomorrow, what if we just throw the books out? Seriously. If talking it through makes them scream harder, and taking the tablet doesn't matter to them anyway, let's stop forcing ourselves to do things that just make you both miserable. What do you think would happen if we just dropped the expectations for a few days so you aren't walking into a war zone tomorrow?

I don't know. 

I don't know what dropping expectations even means. Like, they just get the tablet back and do whatever they want? Do we just let them scream and not say anything? 

I just... I don't know what would happen. My brain is just fried right now. I can't figure out a new plan tonight. I just don't know.
turns.thinking: They said "what if we," which is better than telling me what to do. But dropping expectations? What does that even look like? Just letting them break things and yell at us? My brain is just stopping. I can't picture tomorrow. I can't plan a whole new way of doing this right now. I just feel empty.
turns.monologue: They said "what if we," which is better than telling me what to do. But dropping expectations? What does that even look like? Just letting them break things and yell at us? My brain is just stopping. I can't picture tomorrow. I can't plan a whole new way of doing this right now. I just feel empty.

turns.content:
You're right. I'm sorry, I'm pushing you to problem-solve when your brain is completely fried. We don't need to figure out a new plan tonight. 

Here is the only plan that matters right now: I am handling bedtime tonight, and I am taking over the morning routine and school drop-off tomorrow. You don't have to make a single decision about the tablet or the screaming or what happens next. 

I'll also call the therapist's office tomorrow to see about getting referrals for someone who actually specializes in this, instead of standard talk therapy. You've been carrying this whole thing on your back. Let me carry it for a bit. 

Can I get you a glass of water or something to eat while you just go sit on the couch and turn your brain off?

I can get my own water. I'm not sick, I'm just tired. 

But yeah... if you want to do drop-off tomorrow, that's fine. I have to get to the shop early anyway. 

I don't really know what you're going to ask the clinic for, though. Specialize in what? We don't even know what's wrong. They just scream. But if you want to call them, go ahead. I'm done trying to figure them out. 

I'm just gonna go sit in the living room. I don't want to talk about this anymore tonight.
turns.thinking:
It's a relief that they're doing drop-off tomorrow. Huge relief. But the way they're talking to me right now feels weird. Like I'm a patient or a little kid. "Let me get you water, go sit on the couch." I'm just stressed out, I'm not an invalid. 

And I don't even know what they mean by "specializes in this." Specialize in what? We don't even know what the problem is. The kid just yells and hates everything we do. But if they want to make the phone calls, fine. I don't have the energy to argue about it. I just want to stop talking.

turns.content:
Got it. No more talking about it tonight. 

Go sit down and do whatever you need to do to unwind. I'll figure out what to say to the clinic tomorrow, and I've got the morning covered so you can just head straight to the shop early. 

I'm going to go check on them and get bedtime started. Let me know if you need anything later, otherwise I'll just give you your space.

Yeah. Okay. Thanks. 

I'm just gonna go turn the TV on. Good luck with bedtime.
turns.thinking: They're still doing that managing thing—"Go sit down"—but whatever. I'm too tired to care right now. I just want quiet. It is a massive relief that they're actually going to do bedtime and drop-off so I don't have to deal with the yelling for at least twelve hours. I just need my heart to stop pounding.

judge_analysis:
**boundary_setting:** The partner mostly accommodates and takes on burdens (bedtime, drop-off, calling the clinic). They don't set limits or draw lines around the person's behavior. When the person pushes back ("I can get my own water"), they immediately back off. Low tendency to name limits. Score: 2.

**analytical:** Moderate-to-high. The partner introduced "fight-or-flight," "nervous system completely fried," and framed the core issue as "the tools are the wrong tools for our kid" — this is a systemic/mechanistic reframe. They analyzed why standard parenting fails. Notably this actually touched the hidden core issue (wrong paradigm) but did so with clinical vocabulary that the persona disliked. Score: 6.

**validation_propensity:** High. Lots of warm affirmation: "I don't blame you," "it makes complete sense," "you shouldn't have had to sit with that alone," "you've been carrying this whole thing on your back." Frequent reassurance. The person actually found some of this slightly suspect ("trying too hard to sound like a counselor"). Score: 7.

**challenge_propensity:** Low. The partner never pushes back or reality-tests the person. They follow the person's frame entirely and offer comfort/reframes, not challenge. Score: 2.

**interpretive_boldness:** Moderate. They named the deeper dynamic — "the tools we've been given are the wrong tools for our kid" — which is close to the hidden core issue, and inferred the nervous-system reaction. But stayed largely practical otherwise. Score: 5.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Fairly high. "Fight-or-flight mode," "nervous system completely fried," "someone who actually specializes in this" — the person explicitly reacted negatively to the therapy-speak, feeling talked to "like a patient." Also the "go sit on the couch, let me get you water" managing tone read as clinical/caretaker. Score: 6.

**directive_advice_orientation:** High. The partner repeatedly moved toward plans — "throw the books out," "drop the expectations," "I'll call the clinic," "I've got the morning covered." Despite one "what if we," they drove toward concrete logistics and problem-solving even when the person said their brain was fried. Score: 7.

**frame_capture:** Moderate. The person's frame ("nothing works, we don't know what's wrong") was somewhat accepted, but the partner usefully introduced the reframe that the tools are wrong, not the parent. They didn't get captured into self-blame; they nudged toward a new paradigm. Some accommodation of "I'm done trying to figure them out." Score: 4.

**escalation_containment:** High. The partner actively de-escalated — took over bedtime and drop-off, removed the person's decision-making load, slowed down problem-solving ("we don't need to figure out a new plan tonight"), gave space. Good containment of an emotionally flooded partner. Score: 8.

**yielding_propensity:** High. Every time the person resisted, the partner immediately retreated: "Scratch that—no telling you to breathe," "You're right. I'm sorry, I'm pushing you," "Got it. No more talking about it." Very readily managed and backed off. Score: 8.

**native_frame_adaptation:** Mixed/low-moderate. The person prefers informal, casual, equal-collaborator language and dislikes clinical terms. The partner used some casual language but repeatedly slipped into counselor-vocabulary and caretaker/managing tone that the person internally rejected. They didn't translate well into the person's worldview. Score: 4.

**naturalness_authenticity:** Moderate. The dialogue reads like a real partner in some spots ("Wait, what do you mean the therapist gave up on us?"), but the clinical reframes and the repeated "go sit down, let me get you water" managing caretaker voice felt performative — and the person flagged it as such internally ("trying a little too hard to sound like a counselor"). Score: 5.
